title: How Can a Bridge Hold Up So Much Weight?
question: How can a bridge hold up so much weight?
answer: Bridges hold heavy loads mostly because of their shape. Beams, arches, triangles (trusses) and cables turn weight into squeezing (compression) and pulling (tension). Each part handles the job it is best at, and the weight passes safely into the strong ground at the ends and supports.

visual.what: Huy and Mai stand on a grassy riverbank watching a big truck drive across a road bridge over the river. Mai points at the truck with wide eyes.

parts.text: Huy, look at that truck! It is heavier than an elephant. Why doesn't the bridge just snap?
Great question, Mai. And here is a surprise. In Greece there is a stone bridge about 3,300 years old, and people still use it today.

visual.what: Huy faces the camera with four small icons floating around him. A squeezed spring, a stretched rubber band, a stone arch and a triangle.

parts.text: Today we will find out how a bridge can hold up so much weight. We will meet squeezing, pulling, a clever curve, and a shape that refuses to squash.

visual.what: Mai flexes her arm like a strongwoman. A thought bubble shows a bridge made of huge thick steel bars and giant boulders.

parts.text: Easy! Bridges are made of super strong stuff. Thick steel and giant rocks!

visual.what: On the left, a messy pile of rocks with a question mark. On the right, a single snapped stick of dry spaghetti next to a neat bridge built of spaghetti triangles.

parts.text: That is a smart guess, Mai. Strong materials really do matter, and most big bridges today are made mostly of steel.

But a pile of rocks is not a bridge. And one stick of dry spaghetti snaps easily, yet students build bridges out of spaghetti that are surprisingly strong. So the secret is not just what a bridge is made of. It is also the shape.

visual.what: A side view of a truck on a simple bridge. A big arrow labelled weight points down from the truck, then smaller arrows run along the bridge to both ends and down into the ground, labelled ground.

parts.text: Everything on Earth is pulled down by gravity. That pull is what we feel as weight. A bridge has one big job. Catch that weight and pass it along into the strong ground.

visual.what: On a table, Mai lays a wooden ruler across two stacks of books. A small drawing in the corner shows a plank across a stream.

parts.text: Let's build the simplest bridge, a beam bridge. A beam is just a long, flat piece, like a plank across a stream. Mai, try this ruler.

visual.what: Mai presses one finger on the middle of the ruler and it bends down in a gentle curve between the two book stacks.

parts.text: When I press the middle, it bends!
Yes. The middle is farthest from the supports, so that is where a beam bends the most.

visual.what: A close-up of the bent ruler. Along the top edge, little arrows push towards each other, labelled squeezed. Along the bottom edge, little arrows pull away from each other, labelled stretched.

parts.text: Now look closely. When a beam bends, its top gets squeezed together, and its bottom gets stretched apart. One ruler, two jobs at once.

visual.what: Huy holds up the bent ruler next to a speech card with the number 1 on it.

parts.text: Takeaway one. A bridge must pass weight into the ground, and that squeezes or stretches its parts.

visual.what: Two springs side by side. Hands push the left spring together, labelled compression = squeezing. Hands pull the right spring apart, labelled tension = pulling.

parts.text: Engineers, the people who design bridges, have special words for this. Squeezing is called compression. Pulling and stretching is called tension.

visual.what: Mai squishes a yellow kitchen sponge in one hand, then stretches a rubber band between two fingers, grinning.

parts.text: Compression, squish! Tension, stretch!
Perfect. You sound like an engineer already.

visual.what: A stone block with squeeze arrows and a green tick, then the same stone block with pull arrows, a crack and a red cross. Beside them, a steel bar with green ticks for both.

parts.text: Here is the important part. Stone and brick are very strong when you squeeze them. But pull on them and they crack quite easily. Steel copes well with both.

visual.what: Mai looks worried, holding a small stone. Behind them, an old mossy stone bridge crosses a stream.

parts.text: So stone is bad for bridges?
Not at all! Some stone bridges have lasted thousands of years. Builders just had to find a shape that only squeezes the stone and never pulls it.

visual.what: Huy stands between a squeezed spring and a stretched spring, holding a speech card with the number 2.

parts.text: Takeaway two. Every part of a bridge is squeezed or pulled, so builders pick the right material and the right shape for each job.

visual.what: A stone arch bridge seen from the side. A cart on top pushes down, and arrows follow the curve of the arch around and down both sides into the ground.

parts.text: That shape is the arch. When weight presses on the top of an arch, the curve passes it around and down both sides into the ground.

visual.what: A close-up of the arch showing wedge-shaped stones, each with small arrows pressing into its neighbours. A slice of cake is drawn beside one stone for comparison.

parts.text: An arch is built from wedge shaped stones. A wedge is wide at one end and narrow at the other, like a slice of cake. Each stone presses on its neighbours, so every stone is squeezed. Just what stone likes.

visual.what: The stone arch with the top middle stone glowing gold and labelled keystone. A jigsaw puzzle piece clicks into place beside it.

parts.text: The stone at the very top is called the keystone. It locks all the others in place, like the last piece of a puzzle.

visual.what: The arch with arrows at its feet pushing outward and down. At each end, a big solid block of rock labelled abutment pushes back with its own arrow.

parts.text: An arch also pushes outward at its feet, like your feet trying to slide apart when you stand with your legs wide. So builders put strong blocks at each end, called abutments, to push back and hold the arch together.

visual.what: A heavy wooden cart rolls over an old stone arch bridge. The stones underneath have tiny squeeze arrows and a layer of rubble sits on top of the arch under the road.

parts.text: So if a heavy cart rolls on top, the stones squeeze together even tighter?
Exactly! In old stone arches, more weight made the stones press together harder. Builders even piled rubble, which means broken stones, on top to make the bridge heavier and steadier.

visual.what: A timeline. Far left, a small stone bridge in Greece at about 3,300 years ago. In the middle, a row of Roman arch bridges at about 2,000 years ago. On the right, a car crossing an old Roman arch bridge today.

parts.text: That is why arches last. About 2,000 years ago the Romans built hundreds of stone arch bridges, and many are still standing. Some even carry cars today.

visual.what: Huy traces a curve in the air with his finger, next to a speech card with the number 3.

parts.text: Takeaway three. An arch turns weight into squeezing and sends it down into strong ground at its ends.

visual.what: Huy holds up two frames made of wooden sticks with pins at the corners. One frame is a square and one is a triangle.

parts.text: Now meet a shape that refuses to squash. Here is a square and a triangle made of sticks, with loose pins at the corners.

visual.what: Mai pushes the corner of the square and it leans over into a flat diamond shape. She pushes the triangle and it stays exactly the same.

parts.text: The square flopped into a diamond! But the triangle won't budge!
A triangle cannot change shape unless one of its sides gets longer or shorter. That makes it super stiff.

visual.what: A metal truss bridge made of many triangles, seen from the side. Some pieces are coloured blue with the label squeezed, others red with the label pulled.

parts.text: A bridge made of triangles is called a truss bridge. Each straight piece is mostly just squeezed or just pulled, not bent. And that is exactly what thin pieces handle best.

visual.what: On the left, one spaghetti stick bending and snapping in two. On the right, a spaghetti truss bridge made of triangles holding a small toy car.

parts.text: That is the spaghetti secret. One stick snaps when you bend it. But joined in triangles, lots of weak sticks become one strong bridge. Trusses use material well, so they cost less to build too.

visual.what: Five small bridge drawings in a row, each labelled. Beam, cantilever (arms sticking out from towers), arch, suspension (road hanging from big curved cables), and cable-stayed (straight cables from tall towers).

parts.text: Engineers mix these ideas. There are five main kinds of bridge. Beam, cantilever, arch, suspension, and cable stayed. A cantilever is an arm that sticks out, held at only one end. Suspension and cable stayed bridges hang the road from steel cables, which are great at being pulled.

visual.what: Engineers in hard hats gather around a table with a model bridge, drawings and a small fan blowing at the model.

parts.text: Before a big bridge is built, engineers research, design and test their ideas, often with models. They make sure it can stand up to heavy loads, strong wind, and even earthquakes.

visual.what: Huy holds up the stiff stick triangle next to a speech card with the number 4.

parts.text: Takeaway four. Triangles keep their shape, so a truss turns many thin pieces into one strong bridge.

visual.what: A flat sheet of paper lies across a gap between two stacks of books, sagging in the middle under one coin. Mai frowns at it.

parts.text: Here is a check you can try at home. Lay a sheet of paper across two stacks of books, and put a coin in the middle.
It flopped right down.

visual.what: The same paper folded back and forth into zigzags like a paper fan, lying across the books and holding a little stack of coins. A zoom bubble shows the zigzag folds as little triangles.

parts.text: Now fold the same paper back and forth, like a paper fan, and lay it across again.
It holds lots of coins! The folds make little triangles!

visual.what: A flat sheet of paper on top of a second sheet bent into a curve beneath it, the curve's ends pressed against the book stacks. Coins sit on top, and the books are labelled abutments.

parts.text: Or bend a second sheet into a curve under the flat one, with its ends pushed against the books. Now you have an arch, and the books are your abutments.
Same paper, new shape, much stronger!

visual.what: Huy stands in front of a small arch, a triangle truss and a cable bridge, with arrows flowing from each into the ground.

parts.text: So how does a bridge hold so much weight? With clever shapes. Arches, triangles and cables turn heavy weight into squeezing and pulling, and pass it safely into the ground.

visual.what: The old stone Zhaozhou Bridge in China with one big flat arch and two small open arches in each side, river water flowing through the openings. Mai peeks through one small arch.

parts.text: Fun fact. The Zhaozhou Bridge in China was built of stone about 1,400 years ago, and it still stands. Little extra arches in its sides let floodwater rush through.
A bridge with windows!

visual.what: Huy and Mai stand on a bridge at sunset, looking up at a big airplane flying high overhead. A subscribe button glows in the corner.

parts.text: Huy, if bridges need the ground, how does a giant plane stay up with nothing under it?
Ooh, that is next time's question! Subscribe so you don't miss it. Bye, bridge builders!

facts.claim: A bridge is a structure built to cross a gap such as a river, valley or road.
Possibly the oldest surviving arch bridge, the Arkadiko Bridge in Greece, dates to about 1300 BC (about 3,300 years ago) and local people still use it.
In recent centuries, large bridges are made mostly of steel.
Students build model bridges from spaghetti. A single stick breaks easily if bent, but a truss makes a strong structure from weak pieces.
Gravity pulls things down, and that pull is weight.
Beam bridges are one of the five main types of bridge.
A beam bends most in the middle, between its supports. When it bends, its top is squeezed and its bottom is stretched.
Structural parts can be stressed by tension (pulling) or compression (squeezing).
Stone and brick are strong in compression but cannot resist much tension.
Steel is strong both when squeezed and when pulled.
Some stone bridges have lasted thousands of years.
Masonry arch bridges are designed to stay squeezed (in compression) as much as possible. Arches pass weight down to the supports and push sideways against the abutments at each end.
Roman arch bridges used wedge-shaped arch stones called voussoirs.
In early arch bridges, a keystone in the middle of the bridge bore the weight of the rest of the bridge.
In compression arch bridges, adding weight made the structure stronger. Builders put fill material such as packed rubble above the arch to add weight and stop the arch being pulled.
The Romans built hundreds of stone bridges, for example the Pons Fabricius from 62 BC (about 2,000 years ago). Many still stand and some still carry vehicles.
A triangle made of stiff sticks cannot change shape unless a side changes length, while a square frame can be pushed out of shape.
A truss bridge is made of connected pieces, usually forming triangles. In simple analysis, each piece is only in tension or compression and is not bent.
Truss bridges are cheap to build mainly because they use materials efficiently.
The five major types of bridge are beam, cantilever, arch, suspension and cable-stayed.
The cables of a suspension bridge are in tension (being pulled).
Big structural engineering projects go through research, design, testing and construction. Structures are designed to stand up to gravity loads, wind and natural disasters.

The Zhaozhou Bridge in China, built in 605 CE (about 1,400 years ago), is the oldest arch bridge still standing in China. It has open spandrels (small extra arches in its sides) that let floodwater pass through more easily.

description: How can a bridge carry a truck heavier than an elephant? Huy and Mai find out how squeezing and pulling, arches and triangles let bridges hold huge weights, and some of them have lasted thousands of years. It ends with a safe paper-bridge activity you can do with books and coins at home, which works well for curious kids aged 6 to 12 and for parents and teachers.

cast.name: Huy
cast.role: the host: curious, warm, a little funny; explains

cast.name: Mai
cast.role: an 8-year-old who asks, guesses and tries things
